sentence: Earth spins: at the equator, the ground moves about sixteen hundred seventy kilometers an hour.
claim: At the equator, Earth's rotation carries the surface at about 1,670 km/h (NASA Space Place gives 1,675 km/h).
note: Bible source (§7 #5): 1,675 km/h (1,041 mph). National Geographic (Equator, encyclopedic entry): about 1,670 km/h. Computed: 40,075 km / 23.93 h = 1,674 km/h. Less away from the equator (× cos latitude).

sentence: That beats the speed of sound.
claim: Sound travels about 1,225 km/h in air at sea level and 15 °C, so 1,670 km/h is faster than sound.
source_title: Speed of Sound (NASA education sheet, grades 9–12)
note: Excerpt: sea level 340 m/s, 1225 km/h, 761 mph. 1,670 / 1,225 = 1.36 (Mach 1.4). The air moves with the ground, so no sonic boom (not said). True at the equator; away from it the ground is slower (× cos latitude): it beats sound only below about 43° latitude, so the line stays tied to the equator.

sentence: And Earth circles the Sun at about thirty kilometers every second.
claim: Earth's mean orbital speed is 29.78 km/s.

sentence: Since this began, you've gone farther than New York to Boston.
claim: At 29.78 km/s Earth covers more than 306 km (New York to Boston in a straight line) in the time from the film's start to this line.
source_title: Distance from New York City to Boston (Geodatos)
note: Computed after voicing (compile.py asserts it): 29.78 km/s × t > 306 km for t > 10.3 s; the line is spoken after about 18 s (≈ 540 km). Relative to the Sun. Callback to episode 4's comparison.

sentence: Ptolemy argued that if Earth moved, birds and clouds would be left behind.
claim: Ptolemy (Almagest I.7) argued that if Earth moved, objects not attached to it, such as clouds and birds, would be left behind.
source_title: Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems (Wikipedia)
note: The Dialogue's Second Day answers the classic objections to Earth's motion (falling bodies, birds, clouds). Ptolemy, Almagest I.7, gives the clouds-and-birds argument; an astronomer may prefer to cite it directly.

sentence: In sixteen thirty-two, Galileo answered with a ship's cabin.
claim: In his Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems (1632), Galileo described the cabin below decks of a large ship: flies, butterflies, fish in a bowl and dripping water behave the same whether the ship is at rest or moving smoothly.
note: Excerpt: in the main cabin below decks, flies, butterflies and other small flying animals, a bowl of fish and a dripping bottle behave identically if the ship moves uniformly; the motion is shared by everything, including the air.

sentence: Below deck on calm water, nothing tells you the ship is moving.
claim: Galileo's cabin: below decks, on a ship moving smoothly over calm water, nothing inside (flies, butterflies, fish, dripping water) shows whether the ship is moving.
note: Same passage as c6. 'Calm water' = uniform motion, no rocking.

sentence: You feel a jolt, never a smooth ride.
claim: Smooth, steady motion cannot be felt from inside; only changes (jolts: changes of speed or direction) are felt. Earth's turning and orbit are smooth: we fall freely around the Sun, and the spin's effects are tiny.
note: The reviewer's corrections: 'speed' → any change of motion; we cannot feel the orbit because Earth is in free fall around the Sun (true at any size); the spin can be detected with instruments (Foucault's pendulum, 1851; g about 0.3% weaker at the equator), but not felt.

claim: Speed has meaning only relative to something: you are at rest relative to your chair and moving at about 230 km/s relative to the galaxy's centre (Galilean relativity).
note: The reviewer's fix: Galileo's lesson is that stillness is relative, not an illusion.

sentence: The Sun drags us round the galaxy at about two hundred thirty kilometers a second.
claim: The Sun moves around the centre of the Milky Way at about 828,000 km/h (about 230 km/s; modern estimates about 220–250 km/s).
note: Excerpt: about 515,000 mph (828,000 km/h). Computed: 828,000 / 3,600 = 230 km/s. Other estimates: Live Science 720,000 km/h. Bible §7 #5 [est.].

sentence: One lap: about two hundred thirty million years.
claim: One orbit of the Sun around the galactic centre takes about 230 million years (estimates 225–250 million).
note: Excerpt: roughly 230 million years to complete one orbit. Chandra (NASA/CXC) gives the same; other estimates 225–250 million.

sentence: Last time round, the first dinosaurs had just appeared.
claim: About 230 million years ago, the first dinosaurs had just appeared (the earliest known date to about 231–233 million years, Late Triassic).
source_title: 150 Million Years of Dinosaur Evolution (American Museum of Natural History)
note: Excerpts: the oldest known bones are about 230 million years old (Science News, 'Dawn of the Dinosaurs'); the Natural History Museum (London): the first definitive dinosaurs around 230 million years ago. 'Last time we were here' = one galactic orbit ago (c9); 'here' is where the Sun was relative to the galactic centre, not the same stars (the galaxy's stars move too).

sentence: Light time, across your galactic trip so far: about a twentieth of a second.
claim: At about 230 km/s, by the readout (about 60 s in) the Sun has carried us about 14,000 km around the galaxy; light crosses that in about 0.046–0.048 s.
note: Computed after voicing (compile.py): 230 × t / 299,792 ≈ 1/20 s. The galactic leg only; Earth's orbit and spin point other ways.

sentence: To the galaxy's center: about twenty-seven thousand years.
claim: The Sun is about 27,000 light-years from the galactic centre (8,275 pc), so light from there takes about 27,000 years to reach us.
source_title: The Massive Black Hole (Max Planck Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics, citing GRAVITY Collaboration 2021)
note: The channel's one galactic-centre figure (episode 1, c12).

sentence: So your speed has no single answer.
claim: Speed has meaning only relative to something: you are at rest relative to your chair and moving at about 230 km/s relative to the galaxy's centre (Galilean relativity).
note: The takeaway's first half: speed is relative (c14), so 'how fast are you moving' has no single answer.
